newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi refugees flee from one war zone to another.
newsitem.headline: Burundi refugees flee from one war zone to another.

text.p: An operation to send Hutu refugees fleeing war in Zaire back to their home districts in Burundi stepped up on Tuesday despite aid workers' worries about their safety.

Hundreds of returnees climbed on to buses at Gatumba transit camp on Tuesday to be driven back to the northwestern province of Cibitoke, a no-go area for foreign aid workers and a centre for fighting between Hutu rebels and the Tutsi-dominated army.
"The largest group of people in this camp are from Cibitoke, about 4,400, and that is where we are taking them back," said Dismas Nditabiriye, president of Burundi's official Repatriation Commission.
"There is insecurity in Cibitoke but people have been returning directly across the frontier. Those who can't go home will be looked after by the forces of law and order," he added.

Those heading northeast on U.N.-funded buses originally fled from Burundi to Zaire to escape civil war and massacres in Cibitoke. Human rights groups say both sides to the conflict almost routinely slaughter civilians in reprisal attacks.
Around 11,000 Burundian Hutus have arrived in Gatumba camp in the past 10 days after being ordered to leave Zaire by Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels who have seized much of eastern Zaire.
The returnees fled earlier fighting in Burundi's Cibitoke, Bubanza and rural Bujumbura provinces and aid workers warn it could be difficult to guarantee their security once they return home.
"Last week Cibitoke was tense, but still people are being pushed to go back there," a senior aid worker told Reuters.
Burundian soldiers have started burying at least 31 unidentified bodies found floating in Lake Tanganyika close to the Zairean border, fishermen said on Tuesday.
A total of eleven new corpses were sighted in the lake on Tuesday at the mouth of the Rusizi river, which markes the border between eastern Zaire and western Burundi.
Fishermen, who last week buried about 50 bodies, said the people were probably executed in Cibitoke and dumped in the river. Burundian authorities have denied the army is behind the killings.
More than 150,000 people have been killed in Burundi since the assassination of its first freely-elected Hutu president by Tutsi soldiers in 1993. The army seized power in July in a coup.
